lead: Euler's formula suits a long, slender strut and is hopelessly optimistic for a short, stubby one, which simply squashes. Real columns lie between. The Rankine-Gordon formula blends the crushing load and the Euler load into one curve that is safe at both ends and sensible in between. Medium-length struts — fuselage frame members, landing-gear braces, control linkages — fall in that range.
prereq: You need the Euler load PE and the slenderness ratio λ from Euler buckling of columns and end conditions.

blocks.text: A short column fails by crushing at the squash load P<sub>c</sub> = σ<sub>c</sub> A. Here σ<sub>c</sub> is the crushing stress in N/mm² and A the area in mm². A long column buckles at the Euler load P<sub>E</sub> = π²EI/L<sub>e</sub>², with E in N/mm², I in mm⁴ and L<sub>e</sub> the effective length in mm. A middle column does neither cleanly: it yields a little, bows a little, and fails below both.

Rankine added the reciprocals: 1/P<sub>R</sub> = 1/P<sub>c</sub> + 1/P<sub>E</sub>. This is an empirical rule, not a physical model: it is chosen so that the curve passes through the squash load for a very short column and approaches the Euler load for a long one. Rearranged, P<sub>R</sub> = P<sub>c</sub> P<sub>E</sub>/(P<sub>c</sub> + P<sub>E</sub>).
P<sub>R</sub> = σ<sub>c</sub> A / (1 + a λ²),   a = σ<sub>c</sub> / (π²E)
blocks.where: P<sub>R</sub> is the Rankine-Gordon failure load in N; σ<sub>c</sub> the crushing stress in N/mm²; A the area in mm²; λ = L<sub>e</sub>/r the slenderness ratio; r = √(I/A) the radius of gyration in mm; a the Rankine constant, dimensionless when σ<sub>c</sub> and E share one unit.

blocks.text: The derivation is two lines. Since I = A r², the Euler load is P<sub>E</sub> = π²EA/λ². Put that into P<sub>R</sub> = P<sub>cP</sub>_E/(P<sub>c</sub> + P<sub>E</sub>) and divide top and bottom by P<sub>c</sub>: P<sub>R</sub> = σ<sub>cA</sub>/(1 + σ<sub>c</sub>λ²/(π²E)). So a = σ<sub>c</sub>/(π²E).

At λ = 0 the term aλ² vanishes and P<sub>R</sub> = σ<sub>cA</sub> = P<sub>c</sub>. At large λ, aλ² ≫ 1, so P<sub>R</sub> ≈ σ<sub>cA</sub>/(aλ²) = σ<sub>cA</sub> π²E/(σ<sub>c</sub>λ²) = π²EA/λ² = P<sub>E</sub>. The formula finds both limits on its own, with no switch to throw.

P<sub>R</sub> never exceeds either load. The reciprocal 1/P<sub>R</sub> is larger than 1/P<sub>c</sub> and larger than 1/P<sub>E</sub>, so P<sub>R</sub> is smaller than both. An answer above the Euler load means an arithmetic slip, not a new kind of column.

blocks.where: σ<sub>R</sub> is the average compressive stress at failure in N/mm²; compare it with the allowable stress, not with σ<sub>c</sub> alone.

blocks.text: The constant a normally comes from tests or a handbook, because real struts carry initial bow, residual stress and end restraint that the ideal derivation ignores; a value from σ<sub>c</sub>/(π²E) is only a first estimate. λ must always use L<sub>e</sub> for the actual end conditions, and σ<sub>c</sub> and E must be in the same unit. The result is also called the Rankine formula or the Gordon-Rankine formula.

figure.caption: The steel strut of worked example 1 (A = 400 mm², σ<sub>c</sub> = 320 MPa, E = 200 GPa) at every slenderness. Rankine-Gordon starts at the 128 kN squash load, stays below Euler everywhere, and gives 38.4 kN at λ = 120, where Euler gives 54.8 kN.

spec.aria: Load against slenderness from 0 to 200: a dashed flat line at the 128 kilonewton squash load, a dashed Euler hyperbola falling from above, and the solid Rankine-Gordon curve starting at 128 and staying below both. At slenderness 120 the Euler curve is marked at 54.8 kilonewtons and the Rankine-Gordon curve at 38.4 kilonewtons.

examples.question: A pinned-ended steel strut is 600 mm long, with A = 400 mm², I = 1.0×10⁴ mm⁴, E = 200 GPa and a crushing stress σ<sub>c</sub> = 320 MPa. Find the radius of gyration, the slenderness ratio, the squash load, the Euler load and the Rankine-Gordon load.
steps: Pinned ends give L<sub>e</sub> = L = 600 mm, so λ = L<sub>e</sub>/r = 600/5 = 120, dimensionless.
Squash load: P<sub>c</sub> = σ<sub>cA</sub> = 320 N/mm² × 400 mm² = 128 000 N = 128 kN.
Euler load, with E = 200 GPa = 200 000 N/mm²: P<sub>E</sub> = π²EI/L<sub>e</sub>² = 9.8696 × 200 000 × 1.0×10⁴ / 600² = 54 831 N = 54.8 kN.
examples.answer: P<sub>R</sub> = 38.4 kN, below the Euler load of 54.8 kN and far below the squash load of 128 kN.
examples.check:
import math
A = 400.0      # mm^2
I = 1.0e4      # mm^4
E = 200000.0   # N/mm^2
sc = 320.0     # N/mm^2
Le = 600.0     # mm, pinned ends
r = math.sqrt(I / A)
lam = Le / r
Pc = sc * A
PE = math.pi**2 * E * I / Le**2
a = sc / (math.pi**2 * E)
PR = Pc / (1 + a * lam**2)
print(r)
print(lam)
print(Pc / 1000)
print(round(PE / 1000, 1))
print(round(a, 6))
print(round(PR / 1000, 1))

examples.question: A landing-gear brace is a mild-steel tube, 40 mm outside and 32 mm inside diameter, 2.0 m long and pinned at both ends. Take σ<sub>c</sub> = 320 MPa, the test-based Rankine constant a = 1/7500 for pinned mild steel, and E = 200 GPa. Find the Rankine-Gordon load, the safe load with a factor of safety of 3, and compare with Euler.
steps: Euler: P<sub>E</sub> = π²EI/L<sub>e</sub>² = 9.8696 × 200 000 × 74 192/2000² = 36 612 N = 36.6 kN, just above P<sub>R</sub>, as it must be at this slenderness.
examples.answer: Rankine-Gordon load 34.0 kN, safe load 11.3 kN; Euler gives 36.6 kN. With the theoretical a = σ<sub>c</sub>/(π²E) = 1.62 × 10⁻⁴ the load would be 29.2 kN, so the test constant matters.

traps: Mixing units inside a: σ<sub>c</sub> in MPa and E in GPa gives a that is a thousand times wrong. Convert both to N/mm² first; a itself has no unit.
Using the true length L in λ instead of the effective length Le. Fixed-free, fixed-pinned and fixed-fixed ends all change Le and therefore λ (Euler buckling of columns and end conditions).
Feeding I into λ instead of r. λ = L<sub>e</sub>/r with r = √(I/A); I and r are linked by I = Ar², so I cannot stand in for r.
Getting P<sub>R</sub> larger than P<sub>E</sub> and accepting it. The formula is a reciprocal sum, so P<sub>R</sub> is always the smaller of the two loads — check it before writing the answer.

quiz.q: Write the Rankine-Gordon formula in load form and in stress form, and say what a is.
quiz.a: P<sub>R</sub> = σ<sub>cA</sub>/(1 + aλ²) and σ<sub>R</sub> = σ<sub>c</sub>/(1 + aλ²), with a = σ<sub>c</sub>/(π²E); a is the dimensionless Rankine constant.

quiz.q: What does P<sub>R</sub> tend to as λ → 0 and as λ becomes very large?
quiz.a: As λ → 0, P<sub>R</sub> → σ<sub>cA</sub>, the squash load. As λ grows, P<sub>R</sub> → π²EA/λ², the Euler load.

quiz.q: Explain why P<sub>R</sub> can never be larger than either P<sub>c</sub> or P<sub>E</sub>.
quiz.a: 1/P<sub>R</sub> = 1/P<sub>c</sub> + 1/P<sub>E</sub> is the sum of two positive terms, so it exceeds each of them; inverting, P<sub>R</sub> is less than each. The formula is a fit built to stay below both limits; it does not mean the two modes share the load.

quiz.q: A pinned strut has A = 500 mm², r = 4 mm, L<sub>e</sub> = 800 mm, E = 200 GPa and σ<sub>c</sub> = 300 MPa. Find λ, a and P<sub>R</sub>.
Two struts share the same material and area, one with λ = 30 and one with λ = 150. For which does the Euler formula over-predict the failure load by the larger factor, and why?
quiz.a: For λ = 30. There the Euler load is π²EA/900, many times the squash load σ<sub>cA</sub>, so Euler is wildly unsafe; the Rankine value is close to the squash load. At λ = 150 the two curves nearly meet, so Euler is only slightly optimistic.

quiz.q: A student reports P<sub>R</sub> = 60 kN for a strut whose Euler load is 50 kN. What is wrong?
quiz.a: The answer is impossible, because P<sub>R</sub> must lie below P<sub>E</sub>. Likely causes: λ built from L instead of L<sub>e</sub> on a fixed-free strut (λ too small, so P<sub>R</sub> too large), or σ<sub>c</sub> in Pa against E in N/mm², which makes a a million times too small and P<sub>R</sub> close to the squash load. Note that σ<sub>c</sub> in MPa with E in GPa makes a too large and P<sub>R</sub> too small, so that slip cannot explain it.

beyond: Not for the exam. Design codes use column curves fitted to tests — Perry-Robertson in British practice, the several curves of Eurocode 3 — because one constant a cannot fit every section shape and residual-stress pattern. Rankine-Gordon survives as a fast hand check and as the bridge to inelastic buckling in inelastic buckling. Landing-gear and engine-mount struts are sized with those code curves plus a knock-down for the real end fittings. Search for 'Perry-Robertson formula' and 'column curve imperfection factor' to go further.
